1: Opening (1 minute together with the agenda). The board asked for a USD 250m proposal. One sentence: buy five secondhand ships and keep a small cash reserve, fix three on period charters, trade two spot, and stay out of the large crude tanker market that has already peaked. Base case 19.9% before OPEX, bear case 17.9%. Purchase prices and base-case rates trace to Clarksons SIN sales and fixtures; the MR price is the SIN 5-year-old assessment, because no recent 5-year-old MR sale had a disclosed price. Bear and bull legs use SIN earnings series.
2: Seven parts in the order of the brief: Part 1 answers tasks 1 and 2, Part 2 task 3, Parts 3 and 4 task 4, Part 5 task 5, Part 6 task 6. One chain: the decision needs prices, prices need fundamentals, fundamentals need market confirmation, then we compute earnings, and the shock plan protects the downside.
3: This table is the whole project: how much, why, which data. Why three fixed: in a stress test on SIN weekly spot earnings since 2010 (MR c2010 series 545055, because the MR Eco series starts in 2020; Kamsarmax Eco 533288), three is the fewest that keeps the fleet above 15% before OPEX in the worst 12 months (Nov 2011 to Oct 2012: 15.2% before OPEX, 10.1% after; with two fixed, 13.0% and 7.9%). If each spot ship takes its own worst year separately, 14.6%. Why one MR stays open: MR spot ($53,741) sits 25% above the October 1-year rate ($43,000), so the market expects a fall, the same reading as slide 14. The 1-year rate already prices that fall: in SIN data since 2014, in months when MR spot was 25% or more above the 1-year rate, spot over the next 12 months beat the 1-year rate about half the time (median +4% to +7%; small sample, 12 to 13 months in 7 episodes). So the open ship costs little in expectation, keeps the upside, and fixes if spot stays below $20,000 for 8 weeks. If asked which is the floor: 17.9% is the lowest of our three scenarios (slides 19 and 24, 2025 averages); the stress test is a separate, harsher check. It agrees with slide 20: returns fall below 15% only if the two spot ships together earn under $15,100/day; the 2011 to 2012 pair earned $9,654 + $7,083 = $16,737, below slide 20's grid, which stops at $15,000 + $13,000. Aframax: the 3-year lock gives up about $4.6m of year-one income against the 1-year last done ($53,250, TP Spirit), 1.9 points, to keep income contracted through the wave; each $1,000/day less costs 0.14 points. If asked whether the Aframax curve is steep too: yes, in October 1-year $89,375 against 3-year $37,500, which is why the Aframax takes no spot exposure and is fixed for three years at once. What separates it from Suezmax is price, 1.12x newbuild against 1.44x, and the lowest orderbook of our five segments. If asked about Simandou (slide 10): its ore moves mainly in Capesizes, which tightens the whole bulk fleet.
4: Ship money 245m, cash 5m. Each row names the sale behind the price; for the MRs, with no recent 5-year-old sale at a disclosed price, the SIN assessment. All equity now, leverage optional later. The MRs are a purchase specification: 5-year-old, Eco, Japan or Korea built, for example Clearocean Hickory (2021, HD Hyundai Mipo) or Nord Mirai (2021, Minaminippon). If asked about the October MR assessment of 52m: the same plan would cost 254m; we bid in the 50m to 52m range, and any excess comes from the cash line, which would fall to about 1m; fixed hire adds about 2.7m a month. Section 301: the fees target Chinese-built ships and Chinese owners or operators; with a non-Chinese owner our five ships pay none. If asked about delivery timing: a ship bought in late October delivers in one to three months, and slide 17 removes one twelfth of the year per month of delay.
5: The brief allows buying or chartering, so we costed three routes for both segments. Charter-in keeps only the spread over hire: Kamsarmax +0.35m a year in the base case (+0.49m in the bull case) and a 3.2m loss at 2025 earnings; MR a 1.05m loss in the base case. If asked about our 30/50/20 weights: a chartered-in MR expects about +0.4m a year, against about 10.9m expected from owning one, and at the October 1-year rate of 43,000 the hire exceeds expected earnings. A newbuild earns nothing for 1.5 to 3 years. Secondhand prices in our segments sit at or near replacement cost; Suezmax is far above. If asked about Kamsarmax #2 (2015, 11 years old, against slide 21's 'under 10 years'): it is Japan-built, Eco and scrubber-fitted, on spot the owner keeps the fuel saving, and four of the five ships are under 10 years old.
6: Four trades, one line each. MRs: products trade rebounds 6.3% in 2027 after an 8.9% dip in 2026, so 2027 volume (1,029 Mt) is still about 3% below 2025 (1,062 Mt); the average haul rose 19% from 2019 to 2024 and has been flat since. The spot MR goes where the cargo is, and the bear case already uses 2025 averages. Aframax: fixed for three years at the AET benchmark; we give up spot upside, about 4.6m in year one against the 1-year last done of 53,250 (TP Spirit), to keep income contracted through the wave. Kamsarmax #1: fixed 12 months; the charterer picks bauxite or coal. If asked, Capesizes carry about 90% of Guinea bauxite (SIN #213368); their pull tightens the whole bulk fleet, and Kamsarmax takes the direct Port Kamsar loadings. Kamsarmax #2: Q4 grain, then bauxite and coal, with the BDI 2,000 trigger. Part 3 gives the demand chart behind each trade. Handover to Pricing group B.
7: First price family: purchase prices. Two 2018 Tsuneishi Aframaxes at about 75m (SIN marks them 'region' and 'excess'); two Japan-built Kamsarmax sales on 10 August; the China-built sister sold 2.75m cheaper the next day, a gap that includes port-fee risk and Medi Positano's scrubber. The latest MR sales in the register (7 to 14 Aug) include no 5-year-old ship with a disclosed price, so the MRs use the SIN assessment: 50m in September, 52m in October. If asked whether the Aframax sales (April and May) are stale: SIN September assessments of 85m (5-year-old) and 72.5m (10-year-old) bracket an 8-year-old ship near this level; we price at last done as the brief asks, and the 3-year charter makes the asset financeable.
8: Second price family: charter rates. Every base-case rate is a real fixture from the four weeks before the 12 Sep cut; bear and bull use SIN earnings series. These are benchmarks from other owners' ships; we would fix our own ships at last-done levels with charterers of the same standing. Torm Genesis is 2011-built and got 40,000 for three years on 31 August; ours is 2018-built. CNR means the charterer was not reported. October: MR 1-year 43,000 against the 30,000 in our base, so the MR base case is conservative; a fixture at October levels, or the 2027 renewal, would earn more. The 43,000 is an assessment; we would fix at whatever is done on delivery. Kamsarmax 1-year 19,750 and Aframax 3-year 37,500 sit below our benchmarks. At October assessments the three fixed legs would earn about 2.9m more in total (MR +4.55m, Aframax -0.88m, Kamsarmax -0.79m). On slide 16, read 'Fixed leg has upside' this way. If asked about age: Intensity (2026) and XH Hope (2022) are younger than our Kamsarmaxes; an age discount of 1,000 to 2,000 a day on Kamsarmax #1 would cost 0.14 to 0.28 points (the slide 20 grid varies only the spot ships).
9: Third family: freight rates, the explicit requirement of brief item 3. Our spot Kamsarmax carries Q4 grain and then coal; there is no grain voyage fixture in the cut, so the base keeps the XH Hope rate of 23,000. The coal fixture converts to about 27,400 a day at the September VLSFO average of 874.94 (one route, ballast leg included; a single fixture can sit above the SIN Kamsarmax earnings average, 24,484 in the week of 11 Sep). The MR fixtures cover the Atlantic and intra-Asia. MR spot holds some war premium: it rose from 35,804 to 53,741 between the weeks of 11 Sep and 9 Oct; the bear case uses the 2025 average of 22,950. The Suezmax lines are context only. Count: 16 transactions on slides 7 to 9 plus 1 SIN assessment; the appendix register holds 40. Link: Part 3 asks whether the fundamentals can hold these prices.
